newsitem.title: USA: N.J. Supreme Court hears school financing debate.
newsitem.headline: N.J. Supreme Court hears school financing debate.

text.p: - Advocates of New Jersey's poorest school districts faced off against Gov. Christine Whitman's administration on Tuesday, with both sides offering the state Supreme Court conflicting advice on how to handle school funding.

Lawyers representing the state's 30 poorest school districts urged the court to intervene and order a redistribution of more than $200 million in new funds that concentrates the money in so-called special needs districts.

The state attorney general, Peter Verniero, said the court should recognize that the administration's new financing law was an effort by two co-equal branches of government to comply with a mandate to achieve "substantial parity" in per pupil spending. He also asked the court to withhold judgment until 2001, when the administration plan would be fully in place.
"Education is too important to ask for overnight results," Verniero said.

The three-hour session was to hear arguments on whether the administration's plan would finally settle a 27-year dispute over the disparity in funding and educational outcomes between the state's poorest and most affluent districts. New Jersey's public schools, located in more than 600 local districts, have about 1.1 million students.

The state constitution holds the legislature responsible for supporting a "thorough and efficient system of public schools." Since 1970 the court has held that the state's excessive reliance on local property taxes has allowed an unconstitutional variance to develop.
In 1976, the court ordered schools closed until the state enacted an income tax, but it has since set itself to a more limited goal.
In 1990 it ordered the state to ensure rough parity in the ability of the 30 poorest districts to spend as much as the 120 most affluent districts spend on average.

The Whitman initiative seeks to comply with the mandate by setting outcomes targets, defined curriculum standards and tests to measure achievement, which it defined as meeting the constitutional standard. Then it costed the process and said it would guarantee that amount, leaving local districts on their own resources for extra spending.
Those spending floors range from $6,700 per elementary school pupil to nearly $8,000 for high school students.
The new law also made nearly $200 million available to pay for early childhood education.

David Sciarra of the Education Law Center, which filed the original suit, argued that the new plan was a legal fiction, since it did not guarantee the poor districts the means to meet the goals it set. He asked the court to order a redistribution of all new appropriations, estimated at $287 million.
The court reserved its decision, but it would come under some time pressure if it intended to change the funding formulas. The local districts will finalize their budgets in April.

Not participating was Chief Justice Deborah Poritz. As attorney general, before her appointment as chief justice, Poritz prepared the administration's case in 1994, when the court set the deadline for compliance in September 1997.
